newCitations.caseName: Calista Enterprises, L.L.C. v. Oxford Board of Zoning Appeals
newCitations.citation: 2025-Ohio-1692 (Ohio Ct. App., 12th Dist., Butler County, No. CA2024-09-116, May 12, 2025)
newCitations.outcome: The Twelfth District Court of Appeals reversed the Butler County Court of Common Pleas's affirmance of the Zoning Board's denial of a variance, holding the common pleas court abused its discretion by crediting three of the Board's stated statutory criteria for denial while entirely failing to weigh four other statutory factors that favored granting the variance. The court remanded with instructions that the trial court properly weigh the one valid factor supporting denial against the multiple factors favoring approval -- an interim procedural win for the property owner (variance not yet finally granted, but the denial could not stand on the record as analyzed).
newCitations.notes: Confirmed via the court's own published opinion and independently via Justia/Casemine case summaries.

newCitations.caseName: Craft Custom Homes, LLC v. Zoning Hearing Board of Newtown Township
newCitations.citation: 2025 Pa. Commw. Unpub. LEXIS 27 (Pa. Commw. Ct., Nov. 7, 2024)
newCitations.outcome: The Commonwealth Court affirmed the trial court's reversal of the Zoning Hearing Board's denial of a dimensional variance for 7.5-foot side yards (vs. the required 15 feet) on a small nonconforming residential lot. The court held the parcel had not merged with adjacent commonly-owned parcels under the merger doctrine (a garden and doghouse did not constitute the kind of intensive, unified use required for merger), and that the lot's nonconforming, undersized status created a genuine, non-self-imposed unnecessary hardship justifying the variance. Property owner win; variance ultimately granted.

In an Article 78 proceeding, the Appellate Division annulled the Zoning Board's denial of an area variance, holding the denial was arbitrary and capricious and unsupported by substantial evidence because the Board failed to actually conduct the statutorily-required balancing test under Town Law Section 267-b(3) (weighing benefit to the applicant against detriment to the neighborhood) and instead based its denial on generalized community opposition. Property owner win.
newCitations.notes: Older landmark-level New York area-variance case included because it is a frequently-cited, clean example of the 'community opposition alone is not substantial evidence' doctrine that recurs across many modern variance appeals; full case caption (which town/board) not independently confirmed beyond the citation itself.

newCitations.caseName: Palmer v. Susquehanna Township Zoning Hearing Board
newCitations.outcome: The Commonwealth Court affirmed the Zoning Hearing Board's denial of a variance application, siding with the municipality. Included specifically as a counterweight to the mostly-successful appeals above, since a search focused only on 'variance reversed' language would otherwise skew the sample toward property-owner wins.
newCitations.notes: Case name and disposition ('affirmed') cross-referenced from a secondary legal-search summary and the court's own docket-numbered opinion file, but the full opinion text could not be directly read to confirm every detail -- treat the citation and outcome direction as reliable, but the fact narrative as unconfirmed.

newCitations.caseName: Huntting Hospitality LLC v. Zoning Board of Appeals of the Village of East Hampton
newCitations.citation: 2026 NY Slip Op 50502(U) (N.Y. Sup. Ct., Suffolk Cnty., decided ~April 2026)
newCitations.outcome: A historic inn's owner sought variances for a pool, spa, and patio as part of a larger building-addition application; the Village's ZBA approved the larger addition (including ADA access) but took the position that the accessory-structure area variances for the pool/spa/patio were beyond its authority to decide, effectively refusing to rule on that portion of the application. The court held that refusing to adjudicate the pool variances on the merits would leave the applicant with no avenue for review, and addressed the resulting ripeness/procedural posture in the applicant's favor.
newCitations.notes: Could not directly retrieve and read the full opinion (site blocked automated fetch); outcome description is reconstructed from secondary search snippets and may not capture the court's final disposition precisely. Include with caution -- useful mainly to illustrate that a board's refusal to decide a variance application at all is itself litigable, not as a clean merits data point.

variance_permit_denial_appeal.calibrationNote: The expanded sample (10 cases total: the file's original 5 plus these 5) still skews heavily toward property-owner wins -- roughly 6 of 8 decisive outcomes (Calista, Craft Custom Homes, D'Angelo, plus the original Sam Commercial Properties and Smoking Tree, against only Palmer and Franklin Sq. Realty as clear municipality wins) resulted in the denial being reversed, vacated, or remanded in the applicant's favor. Taken at face value, this suggests baseProbability [0.25, 0.45] may be set too low. But this sample almost certainly still suffers from the same outcome-selection bias flagged elsewhere in this file for spot_zoning_challenge: a routine, correctly-decided variance denial rarely gets appealed to a published opinion or covered by legal press, while a wrongly-denied variance that gets reversed is exactly the kind of case that generates a citable opinion and law-firm blog coverage. Recommend a modest upward nudge (e.g., to roughly 0.3-0.5) rather than a large one, and flagging in the tool itself that the true population of variance denials (most of which are never appealed at all, or are appealed and quietly affirmed without a published decision) is undercounted by any citation-based sample like this one.

newCitations.caseName: Thornber v. Village of North Barrington
newCitations.outcome: Residents challenged the Village's zoning ordinance amendment permitting construction of a cellular telecommunications monopole on municipal property as illegal spot zoning and contract zoning. The Appellate Court upheld the amendment, holding it was not arbitrary or unreasonable because the plaintiffs failed to show any illegal motive by the Village or that the amendment was inconsistent with a comprehensive plan for the property. Municipality win -- the rezoning was upheld.
The North Carolina Court of Appeals invalidated a roughly 29.95-acre rezoning to heavy industrial use as illegal spot zoning. Challenge win -- the rezoning was struck down.
newCitations.notes: Outcome and acreage as summarized by the UNC School of Government's compiled legal summary of North Carolina spot-zoning case law, not independently verified against the full opinion text.

newCitations.outcome: The Court of Appeals held the challenged rezoning was not spot zoning at all, in part because the rezoned area was not limited to a single owner's small parcel. Municipality win -- the rezoning was upheld.
newCitations.notes: Outcome as summarized by the UNC School of Government's compiled legal summary; not independently verified against the full opinion text.

newCitations.caseName: Good Neighbors of Oregon Hill v. County of Rockingham
newCitations.outcome: The Court of Appeals held the challenged rezoning did not constitute spot zoning because the affected parcels were in joint or related ownership rather than the kind of single-beneficiary carve-out the doctrine targets. Municipality win -- the rezoning was upheld.
newCitations.notes: Outcome as summarized by the UNC School of Government's compiled legal summary; not independently verified against the full opinion text.

newCitations.outcome: The Court of Appeals invalidated a rezoning enacted to permit a recycling center as illegal spot zoning. Challenge win -- the rezoning was struck down; industrial/waste-facility fact pattern relevant to commercial/industrial development disputes specifically.
newCitations.notes: Outcome as summarized by the UNC School of Government's compiled legal summary; not independently verified against the full opinion text.

newCitations.outcome: The Court of Appeals upheld a rezoning between similar residential zoning districts, finding it did not amount to illegal spot zoning. Municipality win -- the rezoning was upheld.
newCitations.notes: Outcome as summarized by the UNC School of Government's compiled legal summary; not independently verified against the full opinion text.

spot_zoning_challenge.calibrationNote: This addition materially resolves the outcome-selection-bias concern the file already flags. Pulling from a neutral, systematically-compiled secondary source (UNC School of Government's catalog of North Carolina spot-zoning decisions) rather than searching only for 'spot zoning struck down' headlines, the new 6-case batch splits 2 challenge-wins (McDowell, Etheridge) to 4 municipality-wins (Thornber, Musi, Good Neighbors of Oregon Hill, Childress) -- the opposite skew from the file's earlier pure-search-engine-driven sample. Combined with the file's existing 5 citations (4 invalidated, 1 upheld), the full 11-case sample now runs roughly 6 invalidated (55%) to 5 upheld (45%), which sits comfortably inside, and even validates, the current baseProbability range of [0.3, 0.5] (interpreted as the challenge's success rate) rather than requiring a revision. Recommend leaving the range as-is, and treating this larger, more balanced sample as the reason the earlier bias concern is now substantially, though not perfectly, addressed -- the NC-heavy composition (8 of 11 cases) is a real remaining limitation, since North Carolina's spot-zoning doctrine and the 'fairly debatable'/comprehensive-plan-consistency standards used elsewhere are not identical everywhere.

newCitations.caseName: Masic v. Town of Franklinville, New York
newCitations.outcome: Homeowners alleged Town officials trespassed on their property and selectively enforced zoning and building codes against them out of personal animus in a years-long dispute over their home/barn construction, a small dog-breeding operation, and agricultural activity. On the Town's motion to dismiss, the district court allowed the plaintiffs' federal and state equal protection claims and their federal substantive due process claim to proceed, along with a Monell municipal-liability theory against policymaking officials. This is a procedural win only (surviving a motion to dismiss, not a merits verdict or settlement) -- no damages have been established and the case's ultimate outcome is unknown as of this writing.
newCitations.notes: Included specifically because it shows a plausibly-pled personal-animus/selective-enforcement theory clearing the motion-to-dismiss stage post-2020s, consistent with the file's existing directEvidenceOfDiscriminatoryIntent modifier -- but it is NOT yet a resolved case and should not be treated as a win for calibration purposes until (if) it produces a final judgment or settlement.

newCitations.caseName: Greenbriar Village, LLC v. Mountain Brook City
newCitations.outcome: The Eleventh Circuit expressed reluctance to constitutionalize an ordinary zoning dispute and declined to find a substantive due process or equal protection violation in the City's zoning decision affecting the developer's property. Municipality win.
newCitations.notes: Drawn from a secondary law-firm summary of Eleventh Circuit land-use Section 1983 case law rather than the full opinion; older case (2003) but consistent in direction with the file's existing observation that most Section 1983 zoning claims fail.

section_1983_zoning_claim.calibrationNote: Search-budget constraints cut this category well short of the 4-7 target -- only 2 new citations were found and verifiable, and one of those (Masic) is an unresolved, motion-to-dismiss-stage case rather than a final outcome, so it adds almost no real statistical weight either way. Greenbriar Village adds one more municipality win to the loss column, nudging the file's already-cited '2 of 8 disclosed plaintiff recoveries' pattern toward something like '2 of 9,' which is directionally consistent with, not a challenge to, the current baseProbability [0.1, 0.2]. Bottom line: this pass did not turn up evidence to change the base rate, and the range should be left as-is; it also did not turn up any new large-dollar prevailing-plaintiff case comparable to Del Monte Dunes, Orangetown v. Magee, or W.J.F. Realty, so those three remain the only well-documented anchors for the high end of the damages range -- worth another, better-resourced research pass rather than treating this file's 1983 damages anchor set as complete.

newCitations.caseName: City of Minot v. Cypress Development
newCitations.citation: North Central Judicial District Court, Ward County, N.D., jury verdict July 20, 2021 (docket number not independently confirmed)
newCitations.outcome: The City sued its private development partner for breaching a series of 2011-2015 agreements (development agreement, disposition agreement, lease, and management agreement) covering two downtown mixed-use parking/retail/apartment structures, alleging Cypress failed to make required lease payments and breached construction obligations. Cypress counter-sued for over $50 million, alleging the City's own change in leadership caused it to abandon the project. After trial, the jury found FOR THE CITY and AGAINST the developer, awarding the City $2,442,479.94 in damages for unpaid lease payments and excess/remedial construction costs, and rejected Cypress's $50M+ counterclaim in its entirety. A clean, well-documented example of the reverse fact pattern from most of this claim type's other citations: here it is the MUNICIPALITY recovering from the DEVELOPER for the developer's own breach of a development-related agreement, not the other way around.
newCitations.notes: Well-corroborated by multiple independent local news outlets (Minot Daily News, KX News, KFYR-TV) with a specific, consistent dollar figure, but no court docket/case number or written appellate opinion was located, so treat as a real, credible reported verdict rather than a citable published opinion.

development_agreement_breach.calibrationNote: Search-budget constraints limited this category to a single new citation against the 4-7 target -- a real shortfall worth another research pass. That said, Minot v. Cypress is a genuinely useful, non-trivial addition: every other citation currently in this claim type either has the developer winning outright (Mammoth Lakes, Cle Elum, 5th & Walnut, PML) or involves a different kind of claim (Salem Township recovering for defective public improvements; Hoffman Estates as a reverse-direction municipality-loses case). Minot is the first clean instance in the sample of a municipality affirmatively recovering a large sum FROM a developer for the developer's own breach of development-related agreements -- exactly the kind of case the file's own note says it searched for and could not find on the sideA-breach-losing side. It does not by itself justify changing baseProbability [0.45, 0.7], which describes the developer's OWN claim against the municipality (a different claim direction than Minot), but it is a real, concrete reminder that development-agreement litigation is not one-sided, and if this calculator ever models the municipality's countervailing recovery risk in the same matter, Minot is a strong, well-corroborated anchor for that side of the ledger.
